plan.contextChunk: This figure comprises four reaction energy diagrams arranged in a two-by-two grid and labeled (a), (b), (c) and (d) at their upper left corners. Each panel carries a tall vertical arrow at its left shaded from cream to orange and labeled Energy, a pale blue plotting field, and beneath it a horizontal axis labeled Reaction progress ending in a magenta arrow pointing right; no numbers appear on either axis. Within every field a smooth magenta curve runs from a flat reactant level, over a single rounded maximum, and down to a flat product level. Horizontal dashed lines extend from the reactant level, the top of the maximum, and the product level, and double-headed vertical arrows between those dashed lines are labeled delta G with a double dagger for the barrier height and delta G degree for the overall change. Panel (a) pairs a low barrier with a product level well below the reactants. Panel (b) shows a tall barrier above the same downhill step, its drop to product smaller. Panel (c) has only a shallow hump and ends barely above the reactant level. Panel (d) combines a very tall barrier with a product level clearly above the reactants. Because axes and curve shape stay fixed across the grid, the panels isolate two independently varying quantities: barrier height, and whether products sit above or below reactants. The set establishes that every reaction has its own energy profile.

interactionPlan.concept: A reaction's rate is set by its activation barrier (ΔG‡) while its thermodynamic favorability is set by the product–reactant energy difference (ΔG°), and these two quantities vary independently.

horizontal 'Reaction progress' axis ending in a rightward magenta arrow (no numeric ticks)
pale blue plotting field background
smooth magenta reaction-coordinate curve: flat reactant plateau, single rounded transition-state peak, flat product plateau
dashed horizontal reference line at the reactant energy level
dashed horizontal reference line at the transition-state peak
dashed horizontal reference line at the product energy level
double-headed vertical arrow between reactant line and peak line, labeled 'ΔG‡' (activation barrier)
double-headed vertical arrow between reactant line and product line, labeled 'ΔG°' (overall free-energy change)

interactions.label: Reaction profile
interactions.teaches: The four named archetypes isolate the two independent variables: (a)→(b) raises only the barrier (slower, same ΔG°); (a)→(c) flips only the product level (endergonic, still fast); (d) combines a tall barrier with an uphill step.

interactions.label: Transition-state energy (ΔG‡ peak)
interactions.teaches: Dragging the peak up or down changes ΔG‡ and therefore the rate, while ΔG° (product minus reactant) stays exactly the same — barrier height controls kinetics, not favorability.

interactions.label: Product energy level (ΔG°)
interactions.teaches: Dragging the product plateau above or below the reactant line changes ΔG° and therefore whether the reaction is exergonic or endergonic, while ΔG‡ (peak minus reactant) is unaffected — favorability is independent of rate.

demo_steps.title: Fast exergonic baseline
demo_steps.narration: Panel (a): a low barrier (small ΔG‡) means a fast reaction, and products well below reactants (negative ΔG°) means it is exergonic. Both arrows are short-to-moderate.

demo_steps.title: Raise only the barrier
demo_steps.narration: Switch to slow exergonic (b): the peak climbs so ΔG‡ grows and the reaction slows, but the product level — and thus ΔG° — is unchanged. Same favorability, different rate.

demo_steps.title: Flip only the product level
demo_steps.narration: Switch to fast endergonic (c): the barrier stays shallow (still fast) but the product plateau now sits above the reactants, making ΔG° positive. Rate unchanged, favorability reversed.

demo_steps.title: Tall barrier AND uphill
demo_steps.narration: Slow endergonic (d) combines a very tall ΔG‡ with products above reactants: slow and unfavorable. This is the fourth corner of the two-by-two grid.

demo_steps.title: Explore independence freely
demo_steps.narration: Now drag the two sliders yourself: move the peak while watching ΔG° stay fixed, then move the product level while ΔG‡ stays fixed. The two arrows respond to different sliders, proving the quantities are independent.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: ΔG‡ (barrier height) governs how fast a reaction goes, while ΔG° (product minus reactant energy) governs whether it is favorable — and you can change one without changing the other.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Render a single enlarged reaction-coordinate plot (the toggle selects which archetype is shown, rather than a 2x2 grid). Vertical Energy axis as a cream-to-orange gradient up-arrow on the left; horizontal 'Reaction progress' axis as a magenta right-arrow at the bottom; pale blue plot background; no numeric ticks. The magenta curve is a smooth spline through a flat reactant plateau (fixed baseline ~0.4), a single rounded peak at the barrierHeight value, and a flat product plateau at the productEnergy value. Draw three thin black dashed horizontal lines at reactant, peak, and product levels. Draw a double-headed vertical arrow from reactant line to peak line labeled 'ΔG‡' and another from reactant line to product line labeled 'ΔG°'; recompute and reposition both arrows and the dashed lines live as the sliders move. Use the ‡ and ° symbols in the labels. Keep the curve magenta/pink to match the source figure.

authoredContext:
Not all energy diagrams are like that shown for the reaction of ethylene and HBr. Each reaction has its own energy profile. Some reactions are fast (small ΔG‡) and some are slow (large ΔG‡); some have a negative ΔG°, and some have a positive ΔG°. The figure illustrates some different possibilities.

Some hypothetical energy diagrams: (a) a fast exergonic reaction (low ΔG‡, negative ΔG°); (b) a slow exergonic reaction (high ΔG‡, negative ΔG°); (c) a fast endergonic reaction (small ΔG‡, small positive ΔG°); (d) a slow endergonic reaction (high ΔG‡, positive ΔG°).

Four energy diagrams for different reactions with different values of delta G naught show different magnitudes of activation barrier.
